title: Premortem: The key to ensuring to change sticks?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton describes how he uses a premortem with a head of department before running departmental CPD: asking why, two months on, no one would be doing the proposed change. He walks through a case where a five-part modelling approach was being introduced, listing four predicted barriers (no follow-up, worry about evidence in books, struggling to invent We Do questions, concern for stronger students) and the specific fix for each, such as diarised drop-ins and a supportive headteacher message. The argument is that anticipating failure lets a CPD leader tailor the session so that change survives. The technique is cheap, quick to run, and transferable to any school change initiative beyond CPD.
points: The single premortem question surfaces predictable failure points before the CPD session is written.
Each barrier gets a concrete countermeasure, from calendared drop-ins to securing the headteacher's support on fewer written answers in books.
Barriers can shape the CPD content itself, such as showing what happens when follow-up questions are made up on the spot.
Telling students why Step-by-Step is used pre-empts objections from stronger pupils.
quotes: This is what Dylan Wiliam calls a premortem. It is a fantastic way to anticipate problems before they occur and plan strategies for dealing with them.

Morning lesson drop-ins highlighted that the modelling phase of the lesson was less effective than we both would have liked. The participation ratio was low, and there were few whole-class checks for understanding. As a result, students struggled with the subsequent independent practice, and teachers had to rely on circulation to identify and resolve difficulties.

I organised a quick meeting with the headteacher to see how he would feel if students suddenly had fewer questions in their maths book because teachers were assessing more on mini-whiteboards. He couldn't have been more supportive, and I could share his message to reassure staff in the CPD session.
As I have written about before, I think asking students to copy things down into books has become so ingrained in our practice that we do it without questioning the opportunity cost.

Some students object to the Step-by-Step approach. The best way I have found to counteract this is to tell students exactly why we are doing it—emphasising the importance of setting work out correctly and how easy it is to make little mistakes—and assuring students that they can work at their own speed during the independent practice phase that will follow in a few minutes.
